lines: Money has a price, just like bikes and concert tickets. That price is the interest rate.
When you borrow, you pay it. When you save, you earn it. A higher rate makes borrowing expensive and saving rewarding.
In the United States, one group has its hand on the dial: the Federal Reserve, usually just called the Fed.

The Fed sets one short-term rate, the federal funds rate. That's what banks charge each other to borrow overnight. Every other rate, your car loan, your credit card, your savings account, is stacked on top of it.
The Fed has two jobs. Keep prices stable, which means inflation around two percent. And keep as many people employed as possible.
When inflation runs hot, the Fed raises rates. Borrowing gets pricier, people and businesses spend less, and prices cool off.
When the economy stalls and people lose jobs, the Fed cuts rates. Money gets cheap, spending picks up, and companies start hiring again.
The tricky part is the delay. A rate change can take a year or two to fully kick in. So the Fed is steering a giant ship, guessing where the economy will be, not where it is.
Hit the brakes too hard, and you cause a recession. Too soft, and inflation keeps rolling. Getting it just right is called a soft landing.
So next time you hear the Fed raised rates, you'll know exactly what it means for you: your loans cost more, and your savings earn more.
